name: Calder & Rhys Wool Trenchcoat
description:
A double-breasted wool trench in the classic tradition — belted, storm-flapped, with deep slash pockets and a half-lining in printed silk-analog. Calder & Rhys is a Tier 3 to 4 label that has been making this exact coat in various colorways for forty years. The wool is a medium-weight boiled blend from their New Glasgow mill, substantial enough to cut wind without being stiff. Current season runs in charcoal, toffee, and a deep burgundy that photographs like blood in low light. The collar sits high and wide, and the lapels are cut in a slightly exaggerated proportion that reads as deliberate rather than oversized.

This is the coat you buy when you want to look like you have your life together. Architects wear it. Mid-level corporate analysts wear it. Journalists who cover the Spire but live in Tier 3 wear it. It has no tech features, no embedded sensors — it is simply a very good wool trench made by people who have been making very good wool trenches for a long time. The belt almost always goes untied, draped rather than cinched. It reads as polished and understated, which is exactly the point.
what_it_says: You have taste, you have some money, and you want neither to be immediately obvious.
story_hooks: The burgundy colorway was briefly discontinued after a high-profile Tier 4 executive was photographed wearing one at the scene of a corporate espionage incident — demand quietly doubled
A character inherits one of these from a parent; inside the lining, tucked behind the half-lining stitching, is a folded document that was never meant to be found

Calder & Rhys is rumored to be getting acquired by a Vanthorpe subsidiary, which would end the New Glasgow mill operation — the last independent run of this coat is already being bought up by collectors

physical_description.visual_profile: A timeless double-breasted silhouette with commanding presence—structured shoulders, a mid-thigh length line, and an air of composed authority. The coat reads 'professional with depth,' neither aggressively fashionable nor stubbornly retro. High, wide collar frames the face; exaggerated lapels suggest intentional style without pretension.
physical_description.fit: Tailored but not constraining—room through the chest and shoulders for layering, a subtle taper at the waist. Sleeves hit the wrist bone cleanly. The cut assumes good posture and purposeful movement.
physical_description.primary_material: Medium-weight boiled wool blend from the New Glasgow mill—dense enough to cut wind and weather, with subtle surface texture that catches light unevenly.
physical_description.texture: Smooth with embedded nap; the boiled process gives it a soft, almost suede-like hand despite being wool. Shows wear patterns gracefully—slight shine at stress points becomes a mark of authenticity.
physical_description.color_scheme: Charcoal (primary), toffee, or deep burgundy. Current season emphasizes the burgundy—a color that reads as blood-dark in lowlight, nearly black in shadow but luminous in street-level neon.
physical_description.closures: Six polished button fronts (double-breasted configuration); a soft fabric belt with through-loops, typically worn untied and draped.
distinctive_features: Storm flap detailing across the back shoulders
Half-lining in printed silk-analog with subtle pattern—visible when coat opens
Understated Calder & Rhys woven label at interior neck
No visible tech integration or augmentation ports
Proportioned for layering over light aug-wear or jacket
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 3–4. Accessible to working professionals and mid-tier corporate staff, but signals someone with taste and staying power rather than new wealth.
physical_description.cultural_context: Worn by architects, mid-level analysts, journalists covering the Spire, and anyone who needs to look credible across mixed social tiers. It's the uniform of people building something that matters, or convincing others they are. No street edge; no corpo flash.
physical_description.condition_typical: Broken-in and worn with intention. The belt hangs loose rather than cinched. Slight shine at lapel edges and cuffs from repeated wear. Shows character without looking neglected.
